transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-03-17
Time: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam Ortega (Redwood SE), Sara Patel (Orion - Head of Platform), Diego Marquez (Orion - SRE), Anita Roy (Orion - CTO)

Summary: Quick Optimize walkthrough focused on batching and KV/prefix caching recommendations, cost model tradeoffs for Orion Payments' conversational fraud detection and customer support use cases. Customer requested benchmark plan and security docs.

Topics: Batching behavior, KV cache vs prefix cache, cold-starts, quantization impact, dedicated vs hosted economics, pilot scope, security/compliance questions.

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we, uh, we'll run through the Optimize walkthrough and show some concrete numbers around batching and KV cache. Liam will drive the technical bits.
[00:18] Liam Ortega: hi hi, thanks. quick agenda: baseline perf on your workloads, batching profiles, prefix/KV cache patterns, cost model, recommendations and pilot steps. feel free to interrupt.
[00:35] Sara Patel: thanks, we have about 30k msgs/day right now, mostly short chat turns, some long transcripts for disputes. latency SLO is 350ms p95 for customer-facing flows, cost is big concern.
[00:55] Diego Marquez: also want to make sure anything we store for KV/prefix cache is encrypted and we can rotate keys, and we need audit logs for access.
[01:12] Anita Roy: timeline: want pilot in 2 weeks, decision in 6 weeks. we'll need security review to be done in parallel.
[01:30] Liam Ortega: great. quick clarification: when you say short turns, average token length?
[01:38] Sara Patel: roughly 40 tokens for the prompt, 25 tokens for the model response on average; but dispute flows can be 600-2,000 tokens.
[01:46] Maya Chen: ok, that helps. so two big knobs: batching (how many concurrent requests we combine) and caching (prefix/KV cache to reuse earlier KV cache states). batching reduces per-token cost but can increase tail latency if you wait too long to fill the batch. prefix/KV cache helps long-horizon conversational workloads by saving the KV cache so you don't recompute attention for earlier tokens.
[02:15] Liam Ortega: (shows slide) baseline: hosted model X-4 (open LLM variant) with no caching, single-request latency ~240ms for 65-token output on an A100-like perf. With continuous batching at 20ms collection window and target batch size ~8, throughput improves 3.2x and cost/token drops ~28%, p95 latency moves to ~320ms in our tests.
[02:45] Diego Marquez: 320ms is close to our 350ms p95, we can't go over that. how deterministic are those numbers?
[02:55] Liam Ortega: they're based on similar customers and our perf bench; variability depends on arrival patterns. if arrival rate low you won't form large batches, so batching gains are smaller. we can tune collection window and use latency SLO-aware routing to keep p95 within target.
[03:20] Sara Patel: explain KV vs prefix cache one more time, the difference in cost impact.
[03:27] Liam Ortega: sure. prefix cache is storing commonly repeated prefixes for routes - e.g., standard system prompts or policy text - that we can apply quickly so the model doesn't re-evaluate them. KV cache is the key/value attention cache per session: we can persist the KV state between requests so we avoid recomputing attention for previous tokens. Prefix is lighter and best for static boilerplate; KV cache is where you get big wins for long conversations.
[03:55] Anita Roy: what about security? can KV cache live in customer VPC or is it always stored in Redwood?
[04:03] Maya Chen: for Private deployments we support customer-managed storage in VPC/on-prem. for Dedicated we offer isolated storage with KMS integration. For hosted we encrypt-at-rest (KMS) and provide audit logs; we can discuss a contract addendum for stricter residency.
[04:25] Diego Marquez: rotation and access control?
[04:28] Liam Ortega: KMS supports key rotation, and RBAC ties to our console - you can restrict which routes/services can persist cache. Audit logs include cache reads/writes per session id.
[04:40] Sara Patel: good. can you run a cost model for our mix: 80% short chats, 20% long dispute flows?
[04:48] Liam Ortega: yes. quick back-of-envelope: without cache, cost per long flow ~6x short flow because of tokens; with KV cache persisting between messages you save ~45-60% on long flows depending on how much of the conversation is repeated. combined, you might see overall token cost reduce ~18-25% if we persist active sessions for 24h and your recency pattern holds.
[05:20] Maya Chen: also remember batching affects cost in short-turn-heavy workloads more: short responses benefit from batching because per-request overhead is proportionally larger.
[05:33] [06:00] Speaker 1 (imperfect label): so if we do dedicated capacity, do we get better batching?
[06:05] Liam Ortega: with Dedicated you get reserved GPU pools, more predictable batching because you control concurrency on the instance, and you can tune instance sizes. Dedicated also allows higher per-connection throughput and lower variance in p95. cost model: Dedicated is commit-based, so unit cost per token drops compared to hosted at scale but there's an upfront commitment.
[06:35] Sara Patel: show example numbers for a 3-node dedicated pool vs hosted.
[06:40] Liam Ortega: (shares spreadsheet link) example: for 3xA100 equiv reserved, estimate throughput ~X rps, cost per million tokens about 35% lower vs hosted at your volume, after accounting for infra and infra ops. If traffic spikes, we recommend burst capacity policy to fall back to hosted so you don't degrade availability.
[07:05] Diego Marquez: what about quantization? we are sensitive to small quality regressions on fraud detection prompts.
[07:12] Liam Ortega: quantization (4-bit/8-bit) reduces GPU memory so you can fit larger models or more concurrency; quality drop depends on model type and evals. we recommend running a small eval suite - Redwood Optimize can run regression tests against your prompt set and flag quality delta. for fraud detection, we typically avoid aggressive quantization for core inference until we've validated.
[07:40] [08:10] Maya Chen: ok next section, pilot scope. proposed: 2-week pilot using Dedicated trial (or private if you need VPC), target: reproduce p95 latency <350ms for customer routes and show 20%+ cost reduction via batching+KV cache on dispute flows.
[08:32] Anita Roy: we will need SOC2 docs and encryption specifics before approving Dedicated.
[08:38] Maya Chen: we'll send SOC2 Type II, encryption whitepaper, and a short architecture note on KV storage by EOD 2027-03-18.
[08:52] Diego Marquez: for the pilot, can you instrument token-level cost & latency traces so we can map which prompts drive cost?
[08:58] Liam Ortega: yes, Redwood Console provides per-route token breakdowns and trace hooks; we can enable more verbose tracing for the pilot and redact PII as needed.
[09:18] Sara Patel: latency target for dispute flow is softer: 800ms p95 acceptable if we can massively cut costs, but for customer-facing auth flows must stay under 350ms.
[09:30] Liam Ortega: that's common; we can route high-priority auth flows to low-latency pool with smaller batch windows and no cache if needed, while dispute flows use cached KV to lower cost. This is smart routing.
[09:48] [10:15] Speaker labels get a bit fuzzy here, some overlapping discussion, apologies.
[10:22] Liam Ortega: demo time - I'm going to share a live demo of a micro-benchmark (note: live demo stutter on recording).
[10:30] [10:33] Liam Ortega: (runs benchmark) baseline single request 65-token generation ~245ms, continuous batching at 15ms collection + batch size target 6 => throughput x3 cost down 30% p95 ~305ms. Turning on KV cache for a long session sample reduces compute for repeated context by ~52% in this run.
[11:05] Sara Patel: the KV cache reduction looks great. what's the storage footprint?
[11:10] Liam Ortega: KV cache per session is roughly linear with tokens; for your average session (1,200 tokens) it's ~6-12MB depending on model and kv format; we purge by LRU or TTL (configurable). For 100k active sessions that could be ~600GB which is fine on Dedicated with object storage or VPC-managed store.
[11:38] Diego Marquez: retention & PII concerns - can we scrub or encrypt specific fields before persisting KV?
[11:45] Liam Ortega: you can specify redaction hooks on client side; for server-side we support transformation pipelines before storing cache and field-level encryption/cryptographic transformations via customer KMS in Private.
[12:00] [13:00] Small cross-talk about SLAs and RPO for cache.
[13:12] Anita Roy: what's the failure mode if cache store is unavailable?
[13:17] Liam Ortega: we have graceful fallback - if KV cache lookup fails we fall back to cold-start inference; Redwood supports automatic fallbacks and circuit-breakers, and we can configure retry/backoff to avoid cascading failure. You can set capacity tiers to route to hosted instances if Dedicated cache down.
[13:40] Maya Chen: recap on tuning knobs: batching collection window, max batch size, cache TTL, route-level cache enablement, and model quantization profile.
[13:55] Sara Patel: can you propose concrete defaults for our auth vs dispute flows?
[14:00] Liam Ortega: auth flows: small collection window 5-10ms, max batch size 4, no persistent KV; dispute flows: collection window 20-30ms, batch size 8-12, KV persist TTL 24-72h depending on data classification.
[14:25] [15:05] Diego Marquez: will those batch windows push us over p95 in auth?
[15:10] Liam Ortega: not if we keep window small; also you can use priority queues - auth requests get immediate dispatch lane with lower batching.
[15:20] Sara Patel: we want numbers: cost delta if TTL 24h vs 72h?
[15:27] Liam Ortega: rough: TTL 24h saves 30-40% on long flows; 72h could save up to 55% if conversations reoccur across days. But longer TTL increases storage and data residency considerations.
[15:50] Anita Roy: any compliance red flags with persisting KV for fraud cases?
[15:56] Liam Ortega: main consideration is PII: either redact PII before persisting or use Private deployment so KV never leaves your VPC. Also enforce retention policies and audit. We'll provide a compliance checklist.
[16:20] [17:00] Some small asides: pricing buckets, enterprise discounts.
[17:12] Maya Chen: on pricing, committed Dedicated reduces unit cost; for pilot we can offer a short trial credit and measurement window. I'll include a pricing estimator tailored to your expected daily token volume.
[17:30] Sara Patel: that's helpful. Also curious about model fallbacks: what if you want to fallback to a smaller quantized model to cut cost during peak?
[17:38] Liam Ortega: Redwood supports model variants and smart routing policies - you can define fallbacks that prioritize latency or cost. For example, route to quantized model variant for non-critical flows during peak. We can demo rollback strategies in a technical deep dive.
[18:00] [19:00] Diego Marquez: show me the dashboards we'd get.
[19:05] Liam Ortega: (shares console) per-route token breakdown, p50/p95 latency, per-token cost, and a waterfall showing batching efficiency vs cold-start ratio. You can also create alerts for regression on a given eval prompt set.
[19:40] Sara Patel: any gotchas with session affinity and load-balancing across Dedicated nodes?
[19:46] Liam Ortega: session affinity is recommended for KV cache locality. Redwood's routing can pin sessions to a node pool; we also support redis-based metadata tracking for larger pools. For autoscaling, you can allow rebalance with cache warmup strategies.
[20:10] Maya Chen: ok, let's nail pilot success criteria: 350ms p95 for auth flows, <800ms p95 for dispute flows, and >=20% cost reduction for dispute flows; produce a perf report and cost model at end of pilot.
[20:35] Anita Roy: agreed. we'll sign off if security docs look ok and perf matches.
[20:45] [22:00] A little overlap as people type in chat that they'll review.
[22:10] Liam Ortega: technical note on KV cache shard design: we shard by session id and store metadata for eviction; read/write path is optimized to avoid blocking generation. small chance of mismatch if you run cross-node failover but we guard with consistent hashing.
[22:40] Diego Marquez: ok. curious about memory vs storage tradeoff if we keep cache hot in RAM vs checkpoint to object storage.
[22:48] Liam Ortega: hot RAM is fastest and makes p50/p90 best; object storage rehydrate increases latency for that request. hybrid approach: keep hot set in RAM (recent sessions) and cold persist to object store. eviction policy can be tuned by session activity percentiles.
[23:14] [26:00] Some discussion about expected active session counts and cost.
[26:05] Liam Ortega: for your ballpark of 30k msgs/day and 10k active sessions concurrent peaks, you can run a small Dedicated pool (3 nodes) and still have capacity; exact sizing depends on seq lengths. I'll provide a sizing worksheet.
[26:35] Sara Patel: send sizing worksheet and config example for terraform?
[26:40] Maya Chen: yes, will include example terraform snippets for Dedicated and Private network setup.
[26:55] Anita Roy: ok security touchpoints: SOC2, SAML/SSO integration, KMS and audit logs, penetration test reports?
[27:05] Maya Chen: we'll attach SOC2, SAML doc, KMS integration guide, and pen test summary. we can route pen test questions to our security PM.
[27:25] [30:00] Quick mute/unmute noise.
[30:15] Liam Ortega: returning to cost model - here's an illustrative calculation: baseline hosted cost per 1M tokens = $X (example), with batching + KV for your mix we estimate ~22% cost reduction; Dedicated reserved cuts that per million further by ~30% but adds committed monthly. net cost per token for Dedicated with optimize ~ lower by ~48% vs baseline hosted raw. (numbers are illustrative and we'll send concrete spreadsheet).
[30:52] Sara Patel: can we get per-route billing?
[30:55] Liam Ortega: yes, console supports per-route and per-team cost breakdown.
[31:05] Diego Marquez: any maintenance windows for Dedicated or Private?
[31:09] Maya Chen: we schedule upgrades and offer options for non-disruptive rolling updates. SLA covers scheduled maintenance notifications.
[31:28] Anita Roy: what's the contract minimum for Dedicated?
[31:32] Maya Chen: typically monthly commitments, sliding scale. I'll include the options in the pricing doc.
[31:45] [33:00] Slight pause while files are shared.
[33:10] Sara Patel: ok, shoutouts: want detailed perf logs and the tracer instrumentation.
[33:18] Liam Ortega: we'll include tracing sample and enable extra telemetry for the pilot.
[33:30] Diego Marquez: we'll also want a runbook for cache corruption cases.
[33:36] Liam Ortega: yes, runbook and TTL/eviction knobs included.
[33:50] [35:00] Quick Q&A about data residency in EU - not relevant right now but noted.
[35:12] Anita Roy: will our compliance team need a dedicated rehearsal call?
[35:15] Maya Chen: happy to do a SOC2 deep-dive with your security team next week.
[35:22] Sara Patel: can you include an A/B test plan for trying quantized vs full model on dispute flows?
[35:28] Liam Ortega: yes, we'll include an A/B plan and regression thresholds. Red flags get automatic rollback.
[36:00] [40:00] More wrap-up and scheduling.
[40:05] Maya Chen: recap of next steps: 1) Maya sends pricing + SOC2 + security docs by 2027-03-18, 2) Liam runs perf bench and shares by 2027-03-24, 3) Orion shares traffic sample by 2027-03-22, 4) schedule pilot for week of 2027-03-29.
[40:30] Sara Patel: sounds good.
[40:40] Anita Roy: also please include terraform examples and the sizing worksheet.
[40:45] Maya Chen: will do.
[41:00] Diego Marquez: quick note - we may want Private deployment if audit says KV can't leave our VPC.
[41:05] Maya Chen: understood, we'll layout Private option costs separately.
[41:20] [50:00] Final clarifications and short friendly banter about holidays.
[50:12] Maya Chen: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the docs and next steps.
[50:20] Sara Patel: thanks, this was useful.
[50:25] Anita Roy: thanks all.
[50:30] Meeting end.
